When someone is dispirited, they have lost their enthusiasm, hope, or inner drive — usually because of repeated disappointment, failure, or a situation that keeps beating them down. Think of it this way: a person starts out with spirit — energy, hope, motivation — and then something (or a series of things) drains that spirit away. What's left is a person who feels deflated, discouraged, and low.

The word itself carries that idea right in it: the prefix dis- means "away" or "removed," and spirit refers to inner energy or life-force. So dispirited = someone whose spirit has been taken away from them.
The Feeling — What It's Like to Be Dispirited

Imagine you've been trying really hard at something — studying for an exam, applying for jobs, training for a competition — and despite your efforts, things keep going wrong. At some point, a heavy, drooping feeling sets in. You don't feel angry. You don't feel devastated. You just feel... flat. Hollow. Like the wind has been knocked out of your sails. You start to wonder, what's the point of trying anymore?

That is exactly what being dispirited feels like. It's a quiet, low, downhearted state — not loud or dramatic, but a slow, heavy kind of discouragement that settles over you. A dispirited person might go quiet, lose their usual energy, move more slowly, or stop taking initiative the way they used to.

People usually become dispirited because of things like:

  • Repeated failure or rejection — applying for 50 jobs and hearing nothing back.
  • Lack of results despite real effort — studying hard but still failing.
  • Feeling unappreciated or invisible — working your hardest and no one notices.
  • A long string of bad luck or setbacks — one thing after another going wrong.
  • Harsh criticism or being constantly put down — especially over time.
  • A situation that feels hopeless — like a team that keeps losing, with no sign of improvement.

Notice the common thread: it's rarely one single bad moment that makes someone dispirited. It usually builds up over time through repeated blows to one's hope or confidence.

Dispirited sits in the middle range of emotional intensity — it's not mild, but it's not the most extreme feeling either. Here's a rough picture:

A little discouraged → Dispirited → Despondent → Hopeless/broken

It's stronger than just "feeling a bit tired" or "a little disappointed." But it's not as deep or consuming as despondent (which implies nearly giving up entirely) or clinical depression. Dispirited is more situational — it's connected to specific circumstances, and it can lift when those circumstances change.
How to Use "Dispirited" in a Sentence

Common patterns:

→ feel / look / seem / appear / become + dispirited

  • She felt completely dispirited after failing the exam for the third time.
  • The players looked dispirited as they walked off the field after yet another loss.
  • He gradually became dispirited by the constant rejection.

→ dispirited + noun (describing someone)

  • A dispirited student sat alone in the corner of the library.
  • The dispirited team barely spoke in the locker room.

→ dispirited + by + [the cause]

  • She was dispirited by the lack of any progress.
  • Dispirited by years of trying, he almost gave up on his dream.
Words That Mean Something Similar — And How They Differ

These words are close in meaning to dispirited, but each has a slightly different shade:

Discouraged — Very similar. But discouraged often points to a specific setback ("I'm discouraged by today's result"), while dispirited often implies a deeper, more total draining of one's inner energy. You can be briefly discouraged; being dispirited feels more lasting.

Dejected — Also very close. Dejected often comes after a specific, sudden disappointment (losing a match, getting rejected from a school). Dispirited can be more prolonged — built up over time.

Crestfallen — This describes the immediate, visible slump after a specific disappointment. "She was crestfallen when she didn't get the role." It's more of an in-the-moment reaction. Dispirited is broader and can linger.

Demoralized — Very close to dispirited, but demoralized is often used for groups (an army, a team, a workforce) and implies that the belief in one's own ability to succeed has been shaken. Dispirited works for both individuals and groups.

Despondent — Stronger and darker than dispirited. A despondent person has nearly lost all hope. Dispirited still leaves room for recovery; despondent is closer to giving up entirely.

Downhearted — A softer, more old-fashioned word. It means roughly the same thing but sounds more gentle and is less commonly used in modern writing.

If dispirited means your spirit has been drained away, the opposites describe having spirit in full:

  • Spirited — full of energy and enthusiasm
  • Encouraged — having been given renewed confidence
  • Uplifted — feeling emotionally raised up
  • Buoyant — light, cheerful, and optimistic
  • Motivated / Energized — driven and ready to act
  • Enthusiastic — eager and excited

The same root gives you a small family of words:

  • Dispirit (verb) — to cause someone to lose their enthusiasm or hope.

"The long wait began to dispirit even the most patient volunteers."

  • Dispiritedly (adverb) — in a dispirited manner.

"He stared dispiritedly out the window, unsure of what to do next."

  • Dispiritedness (noun) — the state of being dispirited. (This form is rarely used; instead, people tend to say "a sense of discouragement" or "low spirits.")

Dispirited = having lost your inner hope, energy, or enthusiasm — usually because of repeated setbacks, disappointment, or a draining situation. It describes a quiet, deflated, discouraged feeling: not dramatic, but heavy. The spirit that once drove you forward has been worn away.
